Monks, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

Craving is the cause of suffering and the cause of being bound to the round of birth and death. When the six sense faculties come into contact with the six sense objects, the moment the mind gives rise to attachment and longing, this shows that the mind is already bound by the sense fields, and craving has arisen and been established. One should practice at the very place where mind states arise: wherever craving arises, there one should uproot it and extinguish it.
And, monks, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is the complete abandoning of craving, its cessation, its relinquishing, its renunciation, its release, and its utter non-attachment.
But, monks, where is craving uprooted, and where is craving extinguished?
In the world of body and mind, wherever there is what is enticing and pleasing, that is the very place where craving can be uprooted and extinguished.

Monks, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

The noble truth of the path explains that by cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path one is able to uproot and extinguish craving wherever it arises, thereby bringing suffering to an end. This is the way of the cessation of suffering. The Amitābha Sūtra says:
“In that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

there are always many kinds of wonderful, variegated birds — white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāri, kalaviṅka, and jīvaka, the two-headed birds of shared life. Throughout the six periods of day and night these birds utter harmonious, graceful sounds. Their song proclaims such dharmas as the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path.”
From this we can see the importance of cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path.

And, monks, what is the noble truth of the path that leads to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

And, monks, what is right view? Monks, right view is the knowledge and vision that knows suffering, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path that leads to the cessation of suffering. Monks, this is right view.

And, monks, what is right intention? Monks, right intention is thought that is free from sensual desire and free from attachment to worldly pleasure, and also thought free from hatred and free from violence. Monks, this is right intention.

And, monks, what is right speech? Monks, right speech is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. Monks, this is right speech.
And, monks, what is right action? Monks, right action is abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. Monks, this is right action.

And, monks, what is right livelihood? Monks, right livelihood is when a noble disciple does not earn a living by a wrong way of life but carries on his livelihood in a right way. Monks, this is right livelihood.

And, monks, what is right effort? Monks, a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to preventing unarisen unwholesome actions and unwholesome states of mind from arising; a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to abandoning unwholesome actions and unwholesome states of mind that have already arisen; a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to developing unarisen wholesome actions and wholesome states of mind so that they may arise; a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to sustaining the wholesome states that have already arisen, keeping them from declining and causing them to grow, mature, and reach full development; monks, this is right effort.

And, monks, what is right mindfulness? Monks, a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating the body in the body, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating feeling in feeling, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating mind in mind, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating dharmas in dharmas, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; monks, this is right mindfulness.

And, monks, what is right concentration? Monks, a monk, having abandoned craving and unwholesome states of mind, gives rise to a mind free from sensual desire, accompanied by initial and sustained thought and filled with rapture and bliss, and he enters the first absorption; with the stilling of initial and sustained thought he attains inner calm and one-pointedness of mind, producing a mind free from sensual desire and free of initial and sustained thought, filled with rapture and bliss, and he enters the second absorption; after rapture subsides, he dwells in equanimity, fully mindful and clearly comprehending impermanence, and he experiences in his body the bliss that the noble ones call the pleasure born of mindfulness and equanimity, and he enters the third absorption; having forsaken pleasure and pain, with the earlier rapture and grief also having vanished, he accordingly enters the fourth absorption, which is beyond pleasure and pain and is filled with equanimity and mindfulness. Monks, this is right concentration.

(Initial and sustained thought) 'Initial thought' is directed inquiry — the seeking of truth, the first, rudimentary consideration; 'sustained thought' is sustained examining — the deeper, more refined consideration.
Monks, this is the noble truth of the path that leads to the cessation of suffering.
Thus,

he dwells contemplating dharmas in internal dharmas, contemplating dharmas in external dharmas, and at the same time contemplating dharmas in both internal and external dharmas. Therefore he dwells contemplating the arising of dharmas, he dwells contemplating the passing away of dharmas, and he dwells contemplating dharmas both arising and passing away.
Monks, this is how a monk contemplates dharmas in dharmas, that is, how he contemplates dharmas in terms of the four noble truths.
Monks, anyone who, in this way, rightly cultivates the four establishments of mindfulness for seven years can expect one of two fruits: the highest wisdom in this very life
(the fruit of the arhat)
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of the non-returner
(the fruit of the anāgāmin)

(The four fruits) Practicing the four noble truths yields four fruits: the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat. The first fruit, the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), rendered into Chinese as 'one who enters the stream,' means one who has just entered the stream of the noble ones; the second fruit, the once-returner (sakadāgāmi), rendered as 'one who returns once,' means one who, having reached this fruit, passes away to the heavens and lives there as a celestial being for a single lifetime, then returns once more to this world, and after that no longer comes to be reborn in the sense-desire realm; the third fruit, the non-returner (anāgāmin), rendered as 'one who does not return,' means one who, having reached this fruit, is no longer reborn in the sense-desire realm; the fourth fruit, the arhat, rendered as 'the unborn,' means one who, having reached this fruit, is freed from birth and death, no longer receives a future existence, and attains the highest fruit. (The sense-desire realm) The world in which sentient beings possessed of lust and appetite dwell. (The highest wisdom in this very life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of the non-returner) Attaining the fruit of the arhat in this very life; and if the five aggregates still remain, attaining the fruit of the non-returner (the fruit of the anāgāmin).
Monks, not to speak of seven years — if anyone, cultivating the four establishments of mindfulness rightly in this way for six years, can expect one of two fruits
(the fruit of the arhat and the fruit of the non-returner)
: the highest wisdom in this very life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of the non-returner.

This is why it is said: “Monks, there is but one path that leads beings to purification, that overcomes sorrow and lamentation, that puts an end to suffering and grief, that realizes the truth and attains nibbāna — this path is the four establishments of mindfulness.”
After the Blessed One had spoken thus, the monks were greatly delighted, and they rejoiced in and practiced the Dhamma the Blessed One had taught.
